confucius-17-06b.translation: Respect, and you are not slighted; generosity, and you win people; reliability, and others entrust you; quickness, and there are results; kindness, and you can employ people.
confucius-17-06b.note: Each of the five is given its return.

confucius-17-07a.translation: Bi Xi summoned him and the Master was inclined to go. Zilu said: I once heard you say that a person of character does not enter the house of one who does bad with his own hands. Bi Xi has revolted using Zhongmou. How can you go?
confucius-17-07a.note: The same situation returns and Zilu blocks it again.

confucius-17-07b.translation: He said: yes, I said that. But is it not called hard, that grinding does not wear it thin? Is it not called white, that dyeing does not blacken it? Am I a gourd, to be hung up and never eaten?
confucius-17-07b.note: He does not disown his own words. He stacks another argument on top of them.

confucius-17-08a.translation: You, have you heard of the six words and six cloudings? Not yet. Sit; I will tell you. To love humaneness without loving learning — the clouding is foolishness. To love knowledge without loving learning — the clouding is drifting.
confucius-17-08a.note: For each good quality, the defect that appears when learning is missing.

confucius-17-08b.translation: To love reliability without learning — the clouding is harm. To love straightness without learning — harshness. To love courage without learning — disorder. To love firmness without learning — wildness.
confucius-17-08b.note: The same structure six times. Learning becomes the condition on every quality.

confucius-17-09.translation: My young friends, why do none of you study the Odes? They can rouse you, let you observe, let you join with others, let you voice complaint. Near at hand, serving your father; further off, serving your ruler. And you learn the names of many birds, beasts, plants and trees.
confucius-17-09.note: The uses of poetry listed out, from feeling all the way to natural history.

confucius-17-10.translation: To Boyu he said: have you worked at the Zhounan and the Shaonan? A person who has not is like someone standing with his face to a wall.
confucius-17-10.note: Not having studied is pictured as standing nose to a wall.

confucius-17-11.translation: Ritual, ritual, they say — does it mean jade and silk? Music, music, they say — does it mean bells and drums?
confucius-17-11.note: Strip away the word and the equipment, and he asks what is left.

confucius-17-12.translation: Stern in the face and soft within: compared among lesser men, is he not like the thief who bores through a wall or climbs over it?
confucius-17-12.note: A mismatch between outside and inside is read as an act of not being caught.

confucius-17-13.translation: The village worthy is a pest to character.
confucius-17-13.note: The harshest words go to the state of being disliked by no one.

confucius-17-14.translation: To hear it on the road and tell it on the road is to throw character away.
confucius-17-14.note: Passing on what has been heard without digesting it.

confucius-17-15.translation: Can you serve a ruler alongside a mean man? Before he gets it he frets about getting it; once he has it he frets about losing it. And if he frets about losing it, there is nothing he will not do.
confucius-17-15.note: Where the fear of losing a post will take someone.

confucius-17-16.translation: The ancients had three failings, and today even those seem gone. The ardent of old were unrestrained; today they are dissolute. The proud of old had edges; today they are furious. The foolish of old were straight; today they are merely deceitful.
confucius-17-16.note: Even the same flaw, he says, has got worse with the age.

confucius-17-17.translation: Polished words and a managed expression — humaneness is rare in them.
confucius-17-17.note: The line from Book 1, recorded again unchanged.

confucius-17-18.translation: I hate that purple displaces vermilion, that the tunes of Zheng disorder proper music, that a sharp tongue overturns states and houses.
confucius-17-18.note: Three cases of the counterfeit taking the real one's place.

confucius-17-19.translation: I would rather not speak. Zigong said: if you do not speak, what shall we pass on? The Master said: what does heaven say? The four seasons turn and the hundred things are born. What does heaven say?
confucius-17-19.note: A man who taught by speech all his life reaches for teaching without it.

confucius-17-20.translation: Ru Bei wanted to see Confucius, and Confucius excused himself as ill. As the messenger went out the door, he took up his zither and sang, so that the man would hear.
confucius-17-20.note: He makes sure it is known he is not ill. The refusal is not concealed.

confucius-17-21a.translation: Zai Wo said: three years of mourning is far too long. If a person of character does not practise ritual for three years, ritual collapses; if he does not practise music for three years, music collapses. The old grain is finished and the new is up, the fire-drill turns and the fire is renewed — a year is enough.
confucius-17-21a.note: A proposal to change the institution, brought with its reasons.

confucius-17-21b.translation: The Master said: eating rice and wearing silk — would you be at ease? I would. If you would be at ease, then do it. When a person of character is in mourning, fine food is not sweet to him, music gives no pleasure, his dwelling is not comfortable; that is why he does not.
confucius-17-21b.note: He does not counter with logic. He asks whether it would feel easy, and when the answer comes, he allows it.

confucius-17-21c.translation: If you would be at ease now, then do it. Zai Wo went out. The Master said: how unhumane Yu is. A child is three years old before it leaves its parents' arms. Three years of mourning is the mourning kept everywhere under heaven.
confucius-17-21c.note: Having allowed it to his face, he gives the reason once the man is gone. This is where the number three comes from.

confucius-17-21d.translation: Did Yu not have three years of love from his parents?
confucius-17-21d.note: The ground of the institution is handed back to each person's own memory.

confucius-17-22.translation: Stuffed with food all day and the mind put to nothing — a hard case. Are there not games of chess? Even playing those would be better than nothing.
confucius-17-22.note: Unable to recommend the good thing, he recommends the next best.

confucius-17-23.translation: Zilu said: does a person of character prize courage? The Master said: he puts rightness above it. With courage and no rightness, a person of character makes a revolt; a lesser one becomes a thief.
confucius-17-23.note: To the student who loves courage, he names what ranks above it.

confucius-17-24a.translation: Zigong said: does a person of character also hate things? The Master said: he does. He hates those who publish others' faults, those who slander superiors from below, those with courage and no ritual, those who are bold and blocked up.
confucius-17-24a.note: Asked whether there is anything to hate, he names four.

confucius-17-24b.translation: And you, Si, do you hate anything? I hate those who pilfer and pass it off as knowledge, those who take rudeness for courage, those who take exposing others for straightness.
confucius-17-24b.note: All three the student names are counterfeits of a virtue.

confucius-17-25.translation: Only women and lesser men are hard to keep. Bring them close and they grow familiar; keep them off and they resent it.
confucius-17-25.note: The most disputed line in the book. Some read nuzi as women generally, others as a narrow term for those kept in a household. Either way it does not survive today's standards, and it is given here unaltered rather than hidden.

confucius-17-26.translation: To be disliked at forty — that is the end of it.
confucius-17-26.note: It pairs with the line about forty and fifty in Book 9.

confucius-18-01.translation: Weizi left, Jizi became a slave, Bigan remonstrated and died. Confucius said: Yin had three humane men.
confucius-18-01.note: Leaving, enduring and dying — three different choices, all counted as humaneness.

confucius-18-02.translation: Liuxia Hui was chief judge and was dismissed three times. Someone said: is it not time you left? He said: serving people by the straight way, where would I go and not be dismissed three times? And if I would serve by the crooked way, why leave the land of my parents?
confucius-18-02.note: His reason for staying is not resignation but a calculation.

confucius-18-03.translation: Duke Jing of Qi, considering how to receive Confucius, said: I cannot do as the Ji do; I will treat him between the Ji and the Meng. Then he said: I am old and cannot use him. Confucius left.
confucius-18-03.note: The talk is about how to receive him and ends in not using him. He leaves without a word.

confucius-18-04.translation: The people of Qi sent women musicians; Ji Huanzi accepted them and held no court for three days. Confucius left.
confucius-18-04.note: It ends with the same two words. Leaving needs no long explanation.

confucius-18-05a.translation: Jieyu, the madman of Chu, passed Confucius singing: phoenix, phoenix, how your character has declined. What is past cannot be argued back; what is to come can still be caught. Give it up, give it up. Those who go into government now are in danger.
confucius-18-05a.note: A recluse delivers his advice as a song. The phoenix is Confucius.

confucius-18-05b.translation: Confucius got down to speak with him, but he hurried off and avoided him, and they did not speak.
confucius-18-05b.note: The one who gave the advice refuses the conversation.

confucius-18-06a.translation: Changju and Jieni were ploughing side by side. Confucius passed and sent Zilu to ask where the ford was. Changju said: who is that holding the reins? Kong Qiu. Kong Qiu of Lu?
confucius-18-06a.note: Asked about the ford, he asks back about the man.

confucius-18-06b.translation: He is. Then he knows where the ford is. Zilu asked Jieni, who said: and who are you? Zhong You. A follower of Kong Qiu of Lu? He is.
confucius-18-06b.note: Saying he knows where the ford is, is a jab.

confucius-18-06c.translation: He said: it rolls on and the whole world is like this; who will change it? And rather than follow a scholar who avoids particular men, would you not do better to follow one who avoids the age? And he went on covering the seed without pausing.
confucius-18-06c.note: He gives advice and never stops working. The gesture is the answer.

confucius-18-06d.translation: Zilu went and reported it. The Master said sadly: I cannot flock with the birds and beasts. If I am not of this people's company, whose am I? If the world had the way, I would not be trying to change it.
confucius-18-06d.note: He does not deny the recluse's road. He states where he himself stands.

confucius-18-07a.translation: Zilu had fallen behind and met an old man carrying a basket on a staff. Zilu asked: have you seen my master? The old man said: limbs that do no work, grain you cannot tell apart — who is your master? And he planted his staff and went on weeding.
confucius-18-07a.note: Confucius and his followers seen through the eyes of someone working.

confucius-18-07b.translation: Zilu stood with his hands folded. The old man kept him for the night, killed a chicken and cooked millet for him, and presented his two sons. Next day Zilu reported it. The Master said: a recluse. He sent Zilu back to see him; when he got there the man had gone.
confucius-18-07b.note: He rebukes him and then feeds him well. When they return, he is gone.

confucius-18-07c.translation: Zilu said: not to serve is not right. The order of elder and younger cannot be set aside; how then the duty between ruler and minister? Wanting to keep himself clean, he throws the great bonds into disorder. When a person of character serves, he is carrying out that duty.
confucius-18-07c.note: He answers using the very thing the recluse showed him: his two sons and their order.

confucius-18-07d.translation: That the way will not be carried out — we knew that already.
confucius-18-07d.note: Knowing it cannot be done and doing it anyway turns up here too.

confucius-18-08a.translation: Those who withdrew: Boyi, Shuqi, Yuzhong, Yiyi, Zhuzhang, Liuxia Hui, Shaolian. The Master said: those who did not bend their purpose or disgrace themselves were Boyi and Shuqi.
confucius-18-08a.note: Seven are listed and then graded.

confucius-18-08b.translation: Of Liuxia Hui and Shaolian: they bent their purpose and let themselves be disgraced, but their words matched the norms and their conduct matched their thinking, and that is all. Of Yuzhong and Yiyi: they lived hidden and spoke freely, kept themselves clean, and their withdrawal was well judged.
confucius-18-08b.note: Even for those who bent, he finds what is left and writes it down.

confucius-18-08c.translation: I am different from these: nothing I must do, nothing I must not.
confucius-18-08c.note: He takes none of the seven positions as his own.

confucius-18-09.translation: The grand music master Zhi went to Qi, Gan of the second meal to Chu, Liao of the third to Cai, Que of the fourth to Qin. Fangshu of the drum went to the Yellow River, Wu of the hand-drum to the Han, the junior master Yang and Xiang of the chimes went to the sea.
confucius-18-09.note: A record of musicians scattering. A culture coming apart, written as a list of names.

confucius-18-10.translation: The Duke of Zhou said to the Duke of Lu: a person of character does not abandon his kin, and does not let his great ministers resent being unused. Old associates are not cast off without grave cause, and no one person is required to have everything.
confucius-18-10.note: Four principles of using people, all of them on the side of not discarding.

confucius-18-11.translation: Zhou had eight officers: Bo Da, Bo Kuo, Zhong Tu, Zhong Hu, Shu Ye, Shu Xia, Ji Sui, Ji Gua.
confucius-18-11.note: A record of names and nothing else. One tradition says they were four sets of twins.

confucius-19-01.translation: A scholar gives his life when he sees danger, thinks of what is right when he sees gain, thinks of reverence at sacrifice and of grief in mourning. That will do.
confucius-19-01.note: Four situations, each paired with what to call to mind.

confucius-19-02.translation: Holding to character but not broadly, trusting the way but not deeply — what is there in his presence, and what in his absence?
confucius-19-02.note: Not even worth counting as present or absent.

confucius-19-03a.translation: A student of Zixia asked Zizhang about friendship. Zizhang said: what does Zixia say? He said: associate with those who are fit and turn away those who are not. Zizhang said: that differs from what I heard.
confucius-19-03a.note: Two men taught by the same teacher teach the opposite.

confucius-19-03b.translation: A person of character honours the worthy and makes room for the many, commends the able and pities those who are not. If I am greatly worthy, whom could I not make room for? If I am not worthy, others will turn me away — how should I turn anyone away?
confucius-19-03b.note: Argued from both sides: either way, turning people away is not his place.

confucius-19-04.translation: Even a small art is sure to have something worth seeing in it, but it may mire you if you are going far; so a person of character does not take it up.
confucius-19-04.note: He grants its value and still does not recommend it to someone going a long way.

confucius-19-05.translation: Each day to learn what you did not know, each month not to forget what you could do — that may be called loving learning.
confucius-19-05.note: Gaining and not losing, assigned to the day and to the month.

confucius-19-06.translation: Learn widely and hold your purpose firmly, ask urgently and reflect on what is near — humaneness lies in that.
confucius-19-06.note: Humaneness is not sought separately; it is placed inside the way of studying.

confucius-19-07.translation: The hundred craftsmen stay in their workshops to get their work done; a person of character learns to reach his way.
confucius-19-07.note: Learning compared to a workshop: a place one stays in.

confucius-19-08.translation: When a lesser man errs, he is sure to dress it up.
confucius-19-08.note: The line is drawn not at the error but at what follows it.

confucius-19-09.translation: A person of character changes three times: seen from afar, grave; approached, warm; heard speaking, exacting.
confucius-19-09.note: Looking different at different distances is recorded not as inconsistency but as one man's grain.

confucius-19-10.translation: A person of character gains trust before he puts the people to work; without it they take it as harassment. He gains trust before he remonstrates; without it they take it as slander.
confucius-19-10.note: The same act is read in opposite ways depending on whether trust is there.

confucius-19-11.translation: In the great virtues do not step over the fence; in the small ones a little coming and going is acceptable.
confucius-19-11.note: A line to hold and a line to flex, kept apart.

confucius-19-12a.translation: Ziyou said: Zixia's young students can sprinkle and sweep, answer and come and go — but that is the branch. The root is missing; what then? Zixia heard it and said: ah, Yan You has gone too far.
confucius-19-12a.note: The rebuttal follows a claim that basic training is merely the branch.

confucius-19-12b.translation: In the way of a person of character, what is passed on first and what put off until later? Compare it to plants: they are sorted by kind. How could the way be faked? One who has both the beginning and the end — only a sage.
confucius-19-12b.note: Teaching in an order is not, he answers, a deception.

confucius-19-13.translation: Serve, and if there is room to spare, learn; learn, and if there is room to spare, serve.
confucius-19-13.note: The two are set not in sequence but as a going back and forth.

confucius-19-14.translation: In mourning, reach grief and stop there.
confucius-19-14.note: Not adding procedures but fixing the place to stop.

confucius-19-15.translation: My friend Zhang can do what is hard to do, and yet he is not humane.
confucius-19-15.note: A judgement on a fellow student, left in the record as it was said.

confucius-19-16.translation: How imposing Zhang is. But it is hard to practise humaneness alongside him.
confucius-19-16.note: A second judgement on the same man, set right beside the first.

confucius-19-17.translation: I heard the Master say: people do not give everything of themselves — except, perhaps, at a parent's funeral.
confucius-19-17.note: The man who taught restraint allows one exception.

confucius-19-18.translation: I heard the Master say: in Meng Zhuangzi's filial conduct, the rest could be managed; that he did not replace his father's officers or his father's policies is what was hard.
confucius-19-18.note: The hard part of filial duty is located in leaving the people and the policies in place.

confucius-19-19.translation: The Meng family made Yang Fu chief judge, and he asked Zengzi. Zengzi said: those above have lost the way and the people have long been scattered. When you get at the facts, pity them; do not be pleased.
confucius-19-19.note: Catching someone is not to be treated as an achievement.

confucius-19-20.translation: Zigong said: Zhou's wickedness was not as extreme as all that. This is why a person of character hates to be at the bottom of the stream: all the world's evils drain into it.
confucius-19-20.note: He points at how infamy pools in one place.

confucius-19-21.translation: The faults of a person of character are like an eclipse of sun or moon: when he errs, everyone sees it; when he corrects it, everyone looks up.
confucius-19-21.note: Being visible is not a thing to hide but an opening to correct.

confucius-19-22a.translation: Gongsun Chao of Wei asked Zigong: where did Zhongni study? Zigong said: the way of Wen and Wu has not fallen to the ground; it is in people.
confucius-19-22a.note: Asked where the teacher studied, he answers: in people.

confucius-19-22b.translation: The worthy grasp the large of it, the unworthy the small; there is nowhere the way of Wen and Wu is not. Where did the Master not learn? And what fixed teacher would he have had?
confucius-19-22b.note: Having no fixed teacher is turned around into having learned everywhere.

confucius-19-23a.translation: Shusun Wushu said to the officers at court: Zigong is better than Zhongni. Zifu Jingbo told Zigong. Zigong said: compare it to a courtyard wall. My wall comes to the shoulder; you can peer over and see what is fine in the house.
confucius-19-23a.note: Praised, he answers that his own wall is low.

confucius-19-23b.translation: The Master's wall is many fathoms; unless you find the gate and go in, you do not see the beauty of the ancestral temple or the richness of its officers. Few have found the gate. It is no wonder he said what he said.
confucius-19-23b.note: He does not scold the misjudgement; he says it is only to be expected.

confucius-19-24a.translation: Shusun Wushu disparaged Zhongni. Zigong said: do not. Zhongni cannot be disparaged. Other worthy men are hills, and can be climbed over; Zhongni is sun and moon, and cannot.
confucius-19-24a.note: The same man disparages him a second time, and the image is raised higher.

confucius-19-24b.translation: Though a man cut himself off, what harm is that to sun and moon? It only shows how little he knows his measure.
confucius-19-24b.note: The disparagement exposes not its target but the one doing it.

confucius-19-25a.translation: Chen Ziqin said to Zigong: you are being modest; how could Zhongni be better than you? Zigong said: by one word a person of character is taken for wise, and by one word for unwise. One cannot but be careful with words.
confucius-19-25a.note: Praised, the first thing he says is to be careful what you say.

confucius-19-25b.translation: That the Master cannot be reached is like heaven, which no ladder climbs. Had the Master got a state, it would have been as they say: set them up and they stand, lead them and they go, soothe them and they come, move them and they fall into harmony. In life, honour; in death, grief.
confucius-19-25b.note: Of a man never employed, he speaks in terms of what would have happened if he had been.

confucius-19-25c.note: Book 19 closes on a student's question.

confucius-20-01a.translation: Yao said: ah, you Shun. The count of heaven rests on your person; hold truly to the centre. If the four seas fall into want, heaven's gift ends for good. Shun passed the same charge to Yu.
confucius-20-01a.note: The last book opens with the handing over of rule. The same words are passed on unchanged.

confucius-20-01b.translation: I, the child Lu, dare offer a black bull and announce to the august Lord on high: the guilty I dare not pardon. I will not screen the Lord's servants; the choosing rests in the Lord's heart. If there is guilt in my person, it is not because of the myriad regions; if there is guilt in the myriad regions, the guilt is on my person.
confucius-20-01b.note: The last two clauses, which pull all responsibility onto himself, are the point.

confucius-20-01c.translation: Zhou had great bounty, and good men grew rich. Though there be close kin, they are not like humane men. If the people have faults, they rest on me alone. He made the weights and measures exact, reviewed the laws, restored abolished offices, and government ran in all four quarters.
confucius-20-01c.note: It moves from words to institutions, and the first item is weights and measures.

confucius-20-01d.translation: He revived fallen states, continued broken lines, raised men who had withdrawn, and the hearts of the world turned to him. What he held important: the people, food, mourning, sacrifice. Generosity wins people, reliability makes them entrust, quickness brings results, fairness pleases.
confucius-20-01d.note: The five items from Book 17 come back here as four.

confucius-20-02a.translation: Zizhang asked Confucius: how must one be to take part in government? The Master said: honour the five fine things and keep off the four bad ones. Zizhang said: what are the five fine things?
confucius-20-02a.note: The list is announced first and then unpacked item by item.

confucius-20-02b.translation: A person of character is generous without waste, works people without resentment, wants without coveting, is at ease without pride, commanding without fierceness. Zizhang said: what does generous without waste mean?
confucius-20-02b.note: All five have the same shape: doing it without overdoing it.

confucius-20-02c.translation: Follow what the people find advantageous and make it advantageous to them — is that not generous without waste? Pick the work worth doing and put them to it, and who resents it? Want humaneness and get humaneness — where is the coveting?
confucius-20-02c.note: Three of them unpacked in a row, each as a question turned back.

confucius-20-02d.translation: A person of character slights no one, many or few, small or great — is that not at ease without pride? He straightens his robe and cap and makes his gaze weighty, so that people look and are in awe — is that not commanding without fierceness?
confucius-20-02d.note: Authority is located not in the voice but in dress and gaze.

confucius-20-02e.translation: What are the four bad things? To kill without having taught is called cruelty; to look for results without having warned is called violence; to issue orders late and press the deadline is called injury; and to be stingy in handing over what is going to be given anyway is called miserliness.
confucius-20-02e.note: All four are faults committed by those above.

confucius-20-03.translation: Without knowing the decree there is no being a person of character; without knowing ritual there is no standing; without knowing words there is no knowing people.
confucius-20-03.note: The last passage of the Analects. It closes with three kinds of knowing and what each makes possible.

laozi-01-01a.translation: A way that can be spoken is not the constant way; a name that can be named is not the constant name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things. So in constant desirelessness you see its subtlety; in constant desire you see its edges.
laozi-01-01a.note: From the first sentence it declares that words cannot hold the thing.

laozi-01-01b.translation: These two come from the same source under different names; together they are called the dark. Dark and again dark — the gate of all subtleties.
laozi-01-01b.note: What was split into two is folded back into one.

laozi-01-02a.translation: When everyone knows the beautiful as beautiful, ugliness is already there. When everyone knows the good as good, what is not good is already there. So being and nothing give birth to each other, hard and easy complete each other, long and short measure each other, high and low lean on each other, note and voice harmonise, before and after follow one another.
laozi-01-02a.note: The moment a value is set up, its opposite comes into being with it.

laozi-01-02b.translation: So the sage handles affairs by not acting and teaches without speaking. The ten thousand things arise and he does not turn from them; he gives life and does not possess, acts and does not presume, completes the work and does not stay in it. Just because he does not stay, it does not leave him.
laozi-01-02b.note: The paradox: only by not claiming the achievement does it remain.

laozi-01-03a.translation: Do not exalt the worthy, and the people will not contend; do not prize goods hard to get, and they will not steal; do not display what can be desired, and their hearts will not be disturbed. So the sage governs by emptying their hearts and filling their bellies, weakening their ambitions and strengthening their bones.
laozi-01-03a.note: The cause of competition is located not in people but in what is held up for them.

laozi-01-03b.translation: Keep the people without cunning and without wants, and let the cunning not dare to act. Act by not acting, and nothing is left ungoverned.
laozi-01-03b.note: Not doing nothing: the text says to do not-doing.

laozi-01-04.translation: The way is empty, and using it never fills it. Deep — like the ancestor of the ten thousand things. It blunts the sharp, unties the tangled, softens the glare, settles with the dust. Still — it seems to be there. I do not know whose child it is; it seems to come before the Lord.
laozi-01-04.note: Describing the oldest thing, it never says more than seems.

laozi-01-05.translation: Heaven and earth are not humane; they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. The sage is not humane; he treats the people as straw dogs. Between heaven and earth — is it not like a bellows? Empty and never exhausted, the more it moves the more comes out. Many words run dry fast; better to hold the centre.
laozi-01-05.note: Not playing favourites is what it calls being without humaneness. Not coldness but impartiality.

laozi-01-06.translation: The valley spirit does not die; it is called the dark female. The gate of the dark female is called the root of heaven and earth. Fine and unbroken, it seems to be there; use it and it never tires.
laozi-01-06.note: The empty valley is read as the side that gives birth.

laozi-01-07.translation: Heaven is long and earth lasting. They can be long and lasting because they do not live for themselves, and so they live long. So the sage puts himself behind and finds himself in front, puts himself outside and finds himself preserved. Is it not because he has no private ends that his own ends are accomplished?
laozi-01-07.note: Stepping back turns out to be the method of getting ahead.

laozi-01-08a.translation: The highest good is like water. Water benefits the ten thousand things and does not contend; it settles in the low places people despise, and so it is close to the way. For dwelling, the ground; for the heart, depth; in giving, humaneness; in speech, reliability; in setting right, order; in work, capability; in movement, timing.
laozi-01-08a.note: One image of water carries all seven positions.

laozi-01-08b.translation: Just because it does not contend, there is no fault in it.
laozi-01-08b.note: One line gathers up the seven before it.

laozi-01-09.translation: Better to stop than to hold it brimming; grind it sharp and it will not keep long. Gold and jade filling the hall, no one can guard them; rich and high and proud, you leave your own ruin behind. The work done, withdraw — that is heaven's way.
laozi-01-09.note: Knowing when to step back is given the name of heaven's way.

laozi-01-10a.translation: Carrying your soul and holding to the one, can you keep them from parting? Gathering your breath into softness, can you be an infant? Cleaning the dark mirror, can you leave no flaw? Loving the state and governing the people, can you do it without cunning? With the gate of heaven opening and closing, can you be the female?
laozi-01-10a.note: Five questions, and no answer given.

laozi-01-10b.translation: Clear and reaching all four ways, can you do it without acting? Give life and nurture: give life and do not possess, act and do not presume, raise and do not rule. This is called the dark character.
laozi-01-10b.note: The three clauses from chapter 2 are given a name here: the dark character.

laozi-01-11.translation: Thirty spokes share one hub; it is the emptiness there that makes the cart useful. Clay is worked into a vessel; it is the emptiness there that makes the vessel useful. Doors and windows are cut for a room; it is the emptiness there that makes the room useful. So what is there gives the advantage, and what is not there gives the use.
laozi-01-11.note: Three objects, offered as proof that the hollow is the useful part.

laozi-01-12.translation: The five colours blind the eye, the five notes deafen the ear, the five flavours spoil the mouth; racing and hunting drive the heart wild; goods hard to get warp conduct. So the sage works for the belly and not for the eye: he lets that go and takes this.
laozi-01-12.note: The more stimulation, the duller the sense.

laozi-01-13a.translation: Favour and disgrace are both startling; prize great trouble as you do your own body. What does it mean that favour and disgrace are both startling? Favour is the lower position: get it and you are startled, lose it and you are startled. That is what it means. And what does it mean to prize great trouble as your own body?
laozi-01-13a.note: Favour is not counted as a good. Gaining it draws the same reaction as losing it.

laozi-01-13b.translation: I have great trouble because I have a body; if I had no body, what trouble would I have? So the one who prizes his own person as he prizes the world can be handed the world; the one who loves his own person as he loves the world can be entrusted with it.
laozi-01-13b.note: Entrust it to the one who cares for his own person, not to the one who would spend himself.

laozi-01-14a.translation: Looked at and not seen, it is called even; listened for and not heard, it is called rare; grasped at and not held, it is called fine. These three cannot be pressed further, so they merge into one. Above it is not bright; below it is not dark.
laozi-01-14a.note: Where all three senses fail, a name is put.

laozi-01-14b.translation: Unending, it cannot be named, and returns to no-thing. This is called the shape of no shape, the image of no thing; it is called the blurred. Meet it and you do not see its head; follow it and you do not see its back. Hold the way of old to manage what is here now.
laozi-01-14b.note: Having said it cannot be grasped, it says to govern the present with it.

laozi-01-14c.translation: To know the ancient beginning is called the thread of the way.

laozi-01-15a.translation: Those of old who were good at being scholars were subtle, mysterious, penetrating, too deep to be known. Just because they cannot be known, I will force a description.
laozi-01-15a.note: It says they cannot be drawn and then draws them. The next passage is the drawing.

laozi-01-15b.translation: Hesitant, as crossing a stream in winter; wary, as fearing the neighbours on all sides; dignified, like a guest; loosening, like ice about to melt; solid, like uncarved wood; open, like a valley; mingled, like muddy water. Who can take the muddy and still it so that it slowly clears?
laozi-01-15b.note: After seven images it asks how to clear muddy water. The answer is waiting.

laozi-01-15c.translation: Who can take the settled and move it long so that it slowly comes to life? One who keeps this way does not want to be full. Just because he is not full, he can wear out and not be made new.
laozi-01-15c.note: Clearing and reviving — both go slowly.

laozi-01-16a.translation: Reach utmost emptiness, hold stillness firm. The ten thousand things rise together and I watch them return. Things flourish, and each returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness; it is called returning to what is allotted. That return is called the constant; knowing the constant is called clarity. Not knowing it, you act blindly and badly.
laozi-01-16a.note: Watching things grow, it looks at the side that returns.

laozi-01-16b.translation: Knowing the constant, you make room; making room, you are impartial; impartial, you are whole; whole, you are heaven; heaven, you are the way; the way, you last — and to the end of your days you are not in danger.
laozi-01-16b.note: Six stages linked into a chain.

laozi-01-17.translation: The best: those below know only that he is there. Next, they draw close and praise him. Next, they fear him. Next, they despise him. Where trust is lacking, distrust appears. Unhurried, he is sparing of words; the work is done, the task completed, and the people all say: we did it ourselves.
laozi-01-17.note: The mark of the best rule is not praise but going unnoticed.

laozi-01-18.translation: When the great way fell away, humaneness and rightness appeared. When cunning and cleverness came out, great deceit appeared. When the six relations were not in accord, filial piety and parental love appeared. When states fell into disorder, loyal ministers appeared.
laozi-01-18.note: A virtue being celebrated is read as a symptom of the disease.

laozi-01-19.translation: Cut off sageliness and discard cunning, and the people gain a hundredfold. Cut off humaneness and discard rightness, and the people return to filial love. Cut off skill and discard profit, and there are no thieves. These three are not enough as mere writing, so give them something to belong to: show the plain, hold the uncarved, lessen the private, reduce wanting.
laozi-01-19.note: What the previous chapter called symptoms, this one says to cut off.

laozi-01-20a.translation: Cut off learning and have no cares. Between yes and yeah, how far apart? Between good and bad, how far? What people fear cannot but be feared. Vast — and without end. The crowd is merry, as at a great feast, as climbing a terrace in spring.
laozi-01-20a.note: The description of the world's pleasures is where the isolation of the next passage begins.

laozi-01-20b.translation: I alone am still, without a sign, like an infant that has not yet smiled; weary, as if with nowhere to go home to. The crowd all have more than enough; I alone seem to have lost. Is mine the mind of a fool? Muddled. Ordinary people are bright and clear; I alone am dim.
laozi-01-20b.note: The most personal passage in the book. The word I keeps returning.

laozi-01-20c.translation: Ordinary people are sharp and probing; I alone am dull. Calm, like the sea; blown along, as if never stopping. The crowd all have their uses; I alone am stubborn and coarse. I alone differ from others, and prize being fed by the mother.
laozi-01-20c.note: After the complaint of isolation, the last clause gives the reason for it.

laozi-01-21a.translation: The look of great character follows the way alone. The way as a thing is blurred and vague. Vague and blurred — within it there are images. Blurred and vague — within it there are things. Dim and dark — within it there is essence; and that essence is wholly real, and within it there is trust.
laozi-01-21a.note: Four times it says blurred, and four times it says within it there is.

laozi-01-21b.translation: From now back to antiquity its name has not departed, and by it we survey all beginnings. How do I know the shape of all beginnings? By this.
laozi-01-21b.note: It asks for the grounds and answers only: by this.

laozi-01-22a.translation: Bent, and so whole; crooked, and so straight; hollow, and so full; worn, and so new; little, and so gaining; much, and so confused. So the sage holds to the one and becomes the model for the world. He does not show himself, and so is clear; does not assert himself, and so stands out; does not boast, and so has merit; does not parade himself, and so lasts.
laozi-01-22a.note: The six pairs at the start and the four at the end share one structure.

laozi-01-22b.translation: Just because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him. That old saying, bent and so whole — how could it be empty words? Truly, whole, one returns to it.
laozi-01-22b.note: It quotes an old saying and confirms it is not empty.

laozi-01-23a.translation: Few words are what is natural. A whirlwind does not last a morning, a cloudburst does not last a day. Who makes them? Heaven and earth. If heaven and earth cannot keep it up, how much less a person?
laozi-01-23a.note: The evidence that violent things do not last is taken from the weather.

laozi-01-23b.translation: So one who works at the way becomes the same as the way; one at character becomes the same as character; one at loss becomes the same as loss. To the one who is the same as the way, the way is glad to receive him; the same as character, character is glad; the same as loss, loss too is glad to receive him.
laozi-01-23b.note: Whatever you follow comes out to meet you — loss included, in the same construction.

laozi-01-23c.translation: Where trust is lacking, distrust appears.
laozi-01-23c.note: The line from chapter 17 appears again here.

laozi-01-24.translation: On tiptoe you do not stand; straddling you do not walk. Showing yourself, you are not clear; asserting yourself, you do not stand out; boasting, you have no merit; parading yourself, you do not last. From the way's side these are called leftover food and a growth on the body. Things dislike them, so one with the way does not stay there.
laozi-01-24.note: The four clauses of chapter 22, written out inverted.

laozi-01-25a.translation: There is a thing formed from a mingling, born before heaven and earth. Silent, empty, standing alone and unchanging, moving round and never endangered — it could be the mother of the world. I do not know its name; I style it the way, and forcing a name on it, call it great.
laozi-01-25a.note: It says it does not know the name and then forces one on, twice.

laozi-01-25b.translation: Great means going; going means far; far means returning. So the way is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the king too is great. Within the realm there are four greats, and the king is one of them. People follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the way, and the way follows what is so of itself.
laozi-01-25b.note: The last four clauses climb like steps and stop at what is so of itself.

laozi-01-26.translation: The heavy is the root of the light; the still is the ruler of the restless. So the sage travels all day without leaving the baggage cart. Though there are sights worth seeing, he stays settled and above them. How should the lord of ten thousand chariots treat the world lightly for his own sake? Light, and the root is lost; restless, and the ruler is lost.
laozi-01-26.note: Root and ruler are each set down once at the start and once at the end.

laozi-01-27a.translation: A good traveller leaves no tracks; a good speaker leaves no flaw to fault; a good reckoner uses no counting rods; a good closer uses no bolt and yet it cannot be opened; a good binder uses no cord and yet it cannot be loosed. So the sage is always good at saving people, and so no one is discarded;
laozi-01-27a.note: Five things done without tools, and then it turns to saving people.

laozi-01-27b.translation: Always good at saving things, and so nothing is discarded. This is called inheriting the light. So the good are the teachers of the not-good, and the not-good are the material of the good. Not to value the teacher, not to care for the material — however clever, you are badly lost. This is called the essential subtlety.
laozi-01-27b.note: The lesser side is not to be discarded but kept as material.

laozi-01-28a.translation: Know the male, keep to the female, and be the world's stream. Being the world's stream, the constant character does not leave you, and you return to the infant. Know the white, keep to the black, and be the world's model. Being the model, the constant character does not slip, and you return to the limitless.
laozi-01-28a.note: What you know and what you keep to are set apart: you know the strong side and keep to the weak.

laozi-01-28b.translation: Know the glory, keep to the disgrace, and be the world's valley. The constant character then suffices, and you return to uncarved wood. When the uncarved scatters it becomes vessels; the sage uses them and becomes chief of the officers. So the great cutting does not cut.
laozi-01-28b.note: The chapter closes on the line that the great cutting does not cut.

laozi-01-29a.translation: Whoever would take the world and do something with it, I see that he will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel; it cannot be handled. Handle it and you spoil it; grasp it and you lose it. So things go ahead or follow, breathe out or breathe in, are strong or weak, break or collapse.
laozi-01-29a.note: Four pairs of opposites, shown to make driving it one way impossible.

laozi-01-29b.translation: So the sage lets go of the extreme, the extravagant, the excessive.
laozi-01-29b.note: All three things to be let go are matters of going too far.

laozi-01-30a.translation: One who assists a ruler by the way does not force the world with arms. Such business tends to come back round. Where armies have camped, thorns grow; after a great campaign there is sure to be a year of famine. The good get the result and stop; they do not dare take it as strength.
laozi-01-30a.note: The cost of war is written in soil and harvests.

laozi-01-30b.translation: Get the result and do not parade it; get it and do not boast; get it and do not be proud. Get it because there was no choice; get it and do not make it strength. Things that grow strong grow old: this is called not the way, and what is not the way ends early.
laozi-01-30b.note: The word result is repeated five times, with only what follows it changing.

laozi-01-31a.translation: Fine weapons are instruments of ill omen; things dislike them, so one with the way does not dwell among them. In peace a person of character honours the left; using arms, he honours the right. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the instruments of a person of character; he uses them when there is no choice, and calm detachment is best.
laozi-01-31a.note: It does not regulate how to use weapons but the state of mind for using them.

laozi-01-31b.translation: Victory is not beautiful, and whoever finds it beautiful delights in killing. One who delights in killing cannot get his will in the world. Auspicious affairs honour the left; inauspicious ones honour the right.
laozi-01-31b.note: Taking pleasure in the victory is itself treated as the problem.

laozi-01-31c.translation: The lieutenant stands on the left and the general on the right, which is to say it is conducted as a funeral. Many have been killed, so weep for them in grief; and when the battle is won, conduct it as a funeral.
laozi-01-31c.note: The day of victory is to be handled as a funeral.

laozi-01-32a.translation: The way is always nameless. The uncarved is small, and yet nothing in the world can make it a subject. If lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would come as guests of themselves. Heaven and earth join and sweet dew falls; no one orders the people and they even out by themselves.
laozi-01-32a.note: The weight is on evening out without anyone ordering it.

laozi-01-32b.translation: Once cutting begins there are names; and once there are names, one must know where to stop. Knowing where to stop is how one escapes danger. The way in the world is like streams and valleys running to rivers and the sea.
laozi-01-32b.note: Making names comes with a place to stop making them.

laozi-01-33.translation: Knowing others is wisdom; knowing yourself is clarity. Overcoming others takes force; overcoming yourself is strength. Knowing you have enough is wealth. Acting with effort is having purpose. Not losing your place is lasting. Dying and not perishing is long life.
laozi-01-33.note: Outward and inward are paired off and compared four times.

laozi-01-34a.translation: The great way floods out, going left and right. The ten thousand things lean on it to be born and it does not refuse them; the work is done and it does not call it its own. It clothes and feeds them and does not lord it over them: it may be named small. They all return to it and it does not lord it over them: it may be named great.
laozi-01-34a.note: The same behaviour is called small and called great.

laozi-01-34b.translation: Because it never makes itself great, it can accomplish its greatness.
laozi-01-34b.note: The logic of chapter 7 returns here.

laozi-01-35.translation: Hold the great image and the world comes. It comes and is not harmed; there is calm, evenness, peace. Music and food will stop a passing traveller. The way, coming out of the mouth, is bland and without taste; look and there is not enough to see, listen and not enough to hear, use it and it is never used up.
laozi-01-35.note: Against music and food, it names the way's lack of flavour.

laozi-01-36a.translation: To draw something in, you must first stretch it; to weaken it, first strengthen it; to discard it, first raise it; to take from it, first give to it. This is called subtle clarity. The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.
laozi-01-36a.note: It reads both as a technique of handling people and as the grain of nature.

laozi-01-36b.translation: A fish cannot leave the deep; the sharp instruments of a state cannot be shown to others.
laozi-01-36b.note: A condition attached to using what came before.

laozi-01-37.translation: The way never acts, and nothing is left undone. If lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would transform of themselves. If in transforming desire arose, I would settle it with the nameless uncarved. The nameless uncarved brings freedom from desire. Free of desire, there is stillness, and the world settles of itself.
laozi-01-37.note: The last chapter of the Dao section. It closes on the words of itself.

laozi-02-38a.translation: High character does not make a point of character, and so it has it; low character will not let go of character, and so it has none. High character does not act and has no reason for acting; low character acts and has a reason. High humaneness acts and has no reason; high rightness acts and has a reason.
laozi-02-38a.note: The first chapter of the De section. The moment character is noticed, it stops being character.

laozi-02-38b.translation: High ritual acts, and when no one responds it rolls up its sleeves and drags them in. So when the way is lost there is character; when character is lost, humaneness; when humaneness is lost, rightness; when rightness is lost, ritual. Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust, and the head of disorder.
laozi-02-38b.note: The order the Confucians prize is written out inverted, as a staircase going down.

laozi-02-38c.translation: Foreknowledge is the flower of the way and the beginning of folly. So the great man dwells in the thick and not the thin, in the fruit and not the flower. He lets that go and takes this.
laozi-02-38c.note: Flower and fruit sum up the stages laid out before.

laozi-02-39a.translation: Of old, these got the one: heaven got the one and is clear; earth got the one and is settled; spirits got the one and are numinous; valleys got the one and are full; the ten thousand things got the one and live; lords and kings got the one and set the world right.
laozi-02-39a.note: Six items laid out in the same sentence pattern.

laozi-02-39b.translation: Push it to the end: if heaven could not be clear it might split; if earth could not settle it might burst; if spirits could not be numinous they might cease; if valleys could not fill they might dry; if the ten thousand things could not live they might vanish; if lords and kings could not be exalted they might fall.
laozi-02-39b.note: The same six, inverted and listed once more.

laozi-02-39c.translation: So the noble takes the base as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That is why lords and kings call themselves the orphaned, the widowed, the unworthy. Is that not taking the base as the root? Is it not? So count a carriage part by part and there is no carriage. Do not wish to glitter like jade; be coarse like stone.
laozi-02-39c.note: The ruler's own titles are used as proof of where nobility is rooted.

laozi-02-40.translation: Returning is the way's movement; weakness is the way's use. The ten thousand things of the world are born from being, and being is born from nothing.
laozi-02-40.note: The shortest chapter in the book, and one of the most often quoted.

laozi-02-41a.translation: The best scholar hears the way and works at it; the middling hears it and half keeps it; the lowest hears it and laughs out loud. Without the laughter it would not be enough to be the way. So there are sayings set down: the bright way seems dim, the advancing way seems to retreat, the level way seems rough,
laozi-02-41a.note: Being laughed at is made a condition of its being the way.

laozi-02-41b.translation: High character is like a valley; great whiteness seems soiled; broad character seems insufficient; established character seems slipshod; plain reality seems to shift. The great square has no corners, the great vessel is late in completion, the great note is scarcely heard, the great image has no shape, the way is hidden and without a name. Only the way lends well and completes.
laozi-02-41b.note: Ten items, all of the shape: the greater it is, the less it looks like it.

laozi-02-42a.translation: The way gives birth to one, one to two, two to three, three to the ten thousand things. They carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and the empty breath blends them. What people dislike is just this — orphaned, widowed, unworthy — and yet kings and dukes take these as their titles.
laozi-02-42a.note: After the order of begetting, it comes back down to self-lowering.

laozi-02-42b.translation: So things are sometimes added to by taking away, and taken from by adding. What others teach, I teach too. The violent do not come to their own death — I shall make this the father of my teaching.
laozi-02-42b.note: He first says his teaching is no different from what others teach.

laozi-02-43.translation: The softest thing in the world gallops over the hardest. What has no substance enters where there is no gap; by this I know the benefit of not acting. Teaching without words and the benefit of not acting — few in the world reach them.
laozi-02-43.note: It makes the same point without naming water and rock.

laozi-02-44.translation: Name or person — which is closer? Person or goods — which is more? Gaining or losing — which is the sickness? So excessive love brings great expense, and hoarding brings heavy loss. Know you have enough and nothing shames you; know where to stop and nothing endangers you; and you may last long.
laozi-02-44.note: Three questions, left unanswered, and it moves to the conclusion.

laozi-02-45a.translation: Great completion seems lacking, and its use does not wear out. Great fullness seems empty, and its use is not exhausted. Great straightness seems bent, great skill seems clumsy, great eloquence seems halting. Movement overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat.
laozi-02-45a.note: The shape of chapter 41 returns, now with the use attached to each.

laozi-02-45b.translation: Clear and still sets the world right.

laozi-02-46.translation: When the world has the way, galloping horses are turned back to haul manure. When it does not, war horses foal outside the walls. No calamity is greater than not knowing you have enough; no fault greater than wanting to get. So the sufficiency of knowing you have enough is always sufficient.
laozi-02-46.note: Peace and war are told apart by what the horses are doing.

laozi-02-47.translation: Without going out the door, know the world; without looking out the window, see heaven's way. The further you go, the less you know. So the sage knows without travelling, names without seeing, completes without acting.
laozi-02-47.note: Gathering experience and knowing are placed in opposite directions.

laozi-02-48.translation: Doing learning, you gain daily; doing the way, you lose daily. Lose and lose again, and you arrive at not acting. Not acting, and nothing is left undone. The world is always won by having no business; once there is business, it is not enough to win the world.
laozi-02-48.note: Learning and the way are set apart as adding and subtracting.

laozi-02-49a.translation: The sage has no fixed heart; he takes the people's heart for his own. The good I treat as good; the not-good I also treat as good — character becomes good. The trustworthy I trust; the untrustworthy I also trust — character becomes trustworthy.
laozi-02-49a.note: It chooses not to vary the treatment by who is across from you.

laozi-02-49b.translation: The sage in the world draws in, and for the world he blends his heart. The people all turn their ears and eyes to him, and the sage treats them all as children.
laozi-02-49b.note: Whether treating them as children means lowering or sheltering is read both ways.

laozi-02-50a.translation: Come out and live, go in and die. Those who live are three in ten; those who die are three in ten; and those who live and then move themselves into the ground of death are also three in ten. Why? Because they live their living too thickly.
laozi-02-50a.note: Wanting to live is what carries them to the place of dying.

laozi-02-50b.translation: I have heard that one who keeps life well travels on land and does not meet rhinoceros or tiger, enters an army and wears no armour; the rhinoceros has nowhere to drive its horn, the tiger nowhere to set its claw, the weapon nowhere to put its blade. Why? Because in him there is no ground of death.
laozi-02-50b.note: Not that he avoids them: there is simply no place in him for death to land.

laozi-02-51a.translation: The way gives birth, character nurtures, things give shape, circumstance completes. So among the ten thousand things there is none that does not honour the way and prize character. The honour of the way and the worth of character are not decreed by anyone; they are always so of themselves.
laozi-02-51a.note: It notes that the honour does not come from any decree.

laozi-02-51b.translation: It rears and raises them, settles and ripens them, shelters and covers them. It gives life and does not possess, acts and does not presume, raises and does not rule. This is called the dark character.
laozi-02-51b.note: The three clauses from chapters 2 and 10 appear here a third time.

laozi-02-52a.translation: The world has a beginning, and we take it as the world's mother. Having got the mother, you know the child; knowing the child, return and keep to the mother, and to the end of your days you are not in danger. Block the openings, shut the gate, and all your life you will not toil.
laozi-02-52a.note: It records a round trip: from the child back to the mother.

laozi-02-52b.translation: Open the openings, busy yourself with affairs, and all your life you are past saving. Seeing the small is called clarity; keeping to the soft is called strength. Use the light and return to the brightness, and leave no disaster on yourself. This is called practising the constant.
laozi-02-52b.note: Use the light, it says, and come back to the brightness.

laozi-02-53a.translation: If I had even a little knowledge and walked the great road, my only fear would be straying onto the byways. The great road is very level, and people love the shortcuts. The court is swept clean, the fields are overgrown, the granaries are empty; they wear embroidery, carry sharp swords, are sated with food and drink, and have goods to spare.
laozi-02-53a.note: The tidiness of the court is set beside the ruin of the fields.

laozi-02-53b.translation: This is called the swagger of thieves. It is not the way.
laozi-02-53b.note: A single word delivers the verdict on the description before.

laozi-02-54a.translation: What is well planted is not uprooted; what is well held is not pulled away; and the descendants do not break off the sacrifices. Cultivate it in yourself and the character is true; in the family and it is more than enough; in the village and it grows; in the state and it is abundant;
laozi-02-54a.note: The same act written four times, with only the scope widening.

laozi-02-54b.translation: Cultivate it in the world and the character reaches everywhere. So by the person look at the person, by the family at the family, by the village at the village, by the state at the state, by the world at the world. How do I know the world is so? By this.
laozi-02-54b.note: It closes with the same question and answer as chapter 21.

laozi-02-55a.translation: One who holds character thickly is like a newborn. Wasps and scorpions and snakes do not sting him, fierce beasts do not seize him, birds of prey do not strike him. His bones are weak and his sinews soft, and yet his grip is firm. He does not know the joining of male and female and yet is wholly roused: essence at its utmost.
laozi-02-55a.note: The weakest body is offered as the example of the safest state.

laozi-02-55b.translation: He howls all day and does not go hoarse: harmony at its utmost. Knowing harmony is called the constant; knowing the constant is called clarity. Adding to life is called ill omen; the mind driving the breath is called forcing. Things that grow strong grow old: this is called not the way, and what is not the way ends early.
laozi-02-55b.note: The closing line of chapter 30 returns here unchanged.

laozi-02-56a.translation: Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know. Block the openings, shut the gate, blunt the sharp, untie the tangled, soften the glare, settle with the dust: this is called the dark sameness. So you cannot get close to it, and cannot keep it at a distance;
laozi-02-56a.note: The four clauses of chapter 4 are given a name here: the dark sameness.

laozi-02-56b.translation: you cannot benefit it and cannot harm it, cannot ennoble it and cannot debase it. And so it is prized in the world.
laozi-02-56b.note: Being beyond handling is itself the ground of its worth.

laozi-02-57a.translation: Govern the state by what is straight, use arms by what is odd, win the world by having no business. How do I know it is so? By this. The more prohibitions in the world, the poorer the people; the more sharp instruments the people have, the darker the state; the more skills people have, the more strange goods appear;
laozi-02-57a.note: A chain run four times: the more that is forbidden, the worse it gets.

laozi-02-57b.translation: The clearer the laws and orders, the more thieves there are. So the sage says: I do not act and the people transform themselves; I love stillness and the people set themselves right; I have no business and the people grow rich of themselves; I have no wants and the people become plain of themselves.
laozi-02-57b.note: Four times the same shape: I do not, and the people do of themselves.

laozi-02-58a.translation: When government is muddled, the people are honest; when government is meticulous, the people are deficient. Calamity is what fortune leans on; fortune is where calamity lies hidden. Who knows where it ends? There is nothing fixed. The straight turns odd again, the good turns monstrous again.
laozi-02-58a.note: Calamity and fortune are folded into one place. The best-known passage in the book.

laozi-02-58b.translation: People have been lost in this a very long time. So the sage is square and does not cut, sharp and does not pierce, straight and does not run wild, bright and does not dazzle.
laozi-02-58b.note: All four have the shape of having it and not using it.

laozi-02-59a.translation: For governing people and serving heaven there is nothing like sparing. Only by sparing does one submit early; submitting early is called piling up character; piling up character, there is nothing one cannot overcome; nothing one cannot overcome, and no one knows the limit; no limit known, and one may hold a state;
laozi-02-59a.note: From the single word sparing, a chain is run all the way up to holding a state.

laozi-02-59b.translation: Having the mother of a state, one may last long. This is called deepening the root and firming the stem, the way of long life and long seeing.
laozi-02-59b.note: The image shifts to a tree's roots to close the chapter.

laozi-02-60.translation: Governing a large state is like cooking a small fish. Approach the world with the way and the spirits lose their power — not that they lose it, but that their power does not harm people; and not only does it not harm them, the sage does not harm them either. Since neither harms, character flows back to both.
laozi-02-60.note: Turn it too often and it falls apart. Restraint is part of the governing.

laozi-02-61a.translation: A great state is a low-lying place, the meeting point of the world, the female of the world. The female always overcomes the male by stillness, and by stillness takes the lower place. So a great state that lowers itself to a small one wins the small one; a small state that lowers itself to a great one wins the great one.
laozi-02-61a.note: The formula that the one who lowers wins is applied to both sides.

laozi-02-61b.translation: So one lowers itself and wins, and one lowers itself and is won. The great state only wants to gather and nurture people; the small state only wants to enter and serve. For both to get what they want, the great one should be the one to lower itself.
laozi-02-61b.note: It names which side should lower first: the larger.

laozi-02-62a.translation: The way is the innermost place of the ten thousand things, the treasure of the good and the refuge of the not-good. Fine words can be sold in the market; honoured conduct can be added to others. And if someone is not good, why discard them?
laozi-02-62a.note: The line from chapter 27 about no one being discarded returns here.

laozi-02-62b.translation: So when the Son of Heaven is installed and the three dukes appointed, though there be jade discs presented ahead of teams of four horses, it is not like sitting and offering this way. Why did the ancients prize it? Was it not said that by it the seeker finds and the guilty are spared? And so it is prized in the world.
laozi-02-62b.note: Its value is set by comparison with the most costly gift there is.

laozi-02-63a.translation: Act by not acting, work at no work, taste the tasteless. Treat the small as large and the few as many; repay resentment with character. Plan the hard while it is easy, do the great while it is small; the world's hard things always begin easy, the world's great things always begin small.
laozi-02-63a.note: Repaying resentment with kindness is here. It is the very line the Analects turns down.

laozi-02-63b.translation: So the sage never acts great, and can accomplish greatness. Light promises are sure to be short on trust; treating much as easy is sure to bring much difficulty. So the sage treats things as difficult, and in the end has no difficulty.
laozi-02-63b.note: Treating it as hard turns out to be the method for having nothing hard.

laozi-02-64a.translation: What is at rest is easy to hold; what has not yet shown is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to melt; what is faint is easy to scatter. Act on it before it exists; order it before it is disordered. A tree you can barely reach around grew from a hair's tip; a nine-storey terrace rose from heaped earth;
laozi-02-64a.note: The logic of prevention first, then the images of growth.

laozi-02-64b.translation: A thousand-mile journey starts under your feet. Whoever handles it spoils it; whoever grasps it loses it. So the sage does not handle and does not spoil, does not grasp and does not lose. People fail at their work most often when it is nearly done. Be as careful at the end as at the start, and nothing is spoiled.
laozi-02-64b.note: The most famous line and the most practical advice sit in one paragraph.

laozi-02-64c.translation: So the sage wants to be without wants and does not prize goods hard to get; he learns to be unlearned and returns to what the crowd has passed by. He assists the ten thousand things in being so of themselves, and does not dare to act.
laozi-02-64c.note: Assist and do not act — the whole stance summed up in one clause.

laozi-02-65a.translation: Those of old who were good at the way did not use it to enlighten the people but to keep them simple. People are hard to govern because they have too much cunning. So governing a state by cunning is the state's thief; not governing by cunning is the state's blessing. Knowing these two is also a model.
laozi-02-65a.note: Read by some as keeping people ignorant, by others as refusing a contest of cunning.

laozi-02-65b.translation: Always knowing the model is called the dark character. The dark character is deep and far and runs counter to things, and only then does it reach the great accord.
laozi-02-65b.note: Running counter to things is a summary of the book's method.

laozi-02-66a.translation: Rivers and seas can be king of the hundred valleys because they are good at being below them. So to be above the people you must put yourself below them in words; to be in front of them you must put yourself behind.
laozi-02-66a.note: Water running to the low place and gathering is used as a model of power.

laozi-02-66b.translation: So the sage is above and the people do not feel the weight, is in front and they do not feel harmed. So the world is glad to push him forward and does not tire of him. Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.
laozi-02-66b.note: The closing line of chapter 22 returns here.

laozi-02-67a.translation: Everyone says my way is great and resembles nothing. It is just because it is great that it resembles nothing; if it resembled something, it would long since have become small. I have three treasures I hold and keep: the first is compassion, the second is sparing, the third is not daring to be first in the world.
laozi-02-67a.note: He names three treasures himself — a rare declaration in this book.

laozi-02-67b.translation: Compassionate, and so able to be brave; sparing, and so able to be broad; not daring to be first, and so able to be chief of the vessels. To abandon compassion for bravery, sparing for breadth, the rear for the front — that is death. Fight with compassion and you win; defend with it and you hold.
laozi-02-67b.note: Compassion is named as a condition for war.

laozi-02-67c.translation: When heaven would save someone, it guards them with compassion.
laozi-02-67c.note: Two clauses close the passage on the three treasures.

laozi-02-68.translation: One good at being a scholar is not warlike; one good at fighting does not rage; one good at overcoming the enemy does not engage; one good at using people puts himself below them. This is called the character of not contending, the use of others' strength, matching heaven, the utmost of old.
laozi-02-68.note: All four kinds of being good are written as not doing.

laozi-02-69a.translation: There is a saying on using arms: I do not dare be the host but the guest; I do not dare advance an inch but retreat a foot. This is called marching without marching, rolling up a sleeve with no arm, dragging with no enemy, taking hold with no weapon. No calamity is greater than making light of the enemy; make light of the enemy and I lose my treasures.
laozi-02-69a.note: The three treasures of the chapter before return here as what is lost.

laozi-02-69b.translation: So when armies are matched against each other, the side that grieves wins.
laozi-02-69b.note: The condition for winning is written as grief.

laozi-02-70.translation: My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practise, and the world can neither understand nor practise them. Words have an ancestor; affairs have a ruler. Just because they do not know, they do not know me. Those who know me are few, and those who take me as a model are rare. So the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside.
laozi-02-70.note: A complaint about not being known, closing on jade carried under the coat.

laozi-02-71.translation: To know and to think you do not is best; not to know and to think you do is the sickness. Only by taking the sickness as sickness is one not sick. The sage is not sick because he takes the sickness as sickness.
laozi-02-71.note: The word sickness is used six times and the sentence turns a full circle.

laozi-02-72.translation: When the people do not fear authority, a greater authority arrives. Do not crowd the places they live, do not make them sick of their livelihood. Only by not making them sick of it are they not sick of you. So the sage knows himself and does not display himself, loves himself and does not call himself noble; he lets that go and takes this.
laozi-02-72.note: A warning: push past a limit and the fear stops working.

laozi-02-73a.translation: Bold in daring, and you are killed; bold in not daring, and you live. Of these two, one benefits and one harms. What heaven dislikes — who knows the reason? So even the sage finds it difficult.
laozi-02-73a.note: A rare passage where even the sage is said not to know.

laozi-02-73b.translation: Heaven's way does not contend and wins well, does not speak and answers well, is not summoned and comes of itself, is unhurried and plans well. Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, and nothing slips through.
laozi-02-73b.note: Slow and wide-meshed, and missing nothing — held in the same place.

laozi-02-74a.translation: If the people do not fear death, how will you frighten them with it? Suppose the people always feared death, and I could seize and kill whoever did something strange — who would dare? There is always the one in charge of killing who kills; to kill in place of the one in charge is to hew in place of the master carpenter.
laozi-02-74a.note: The office of putting to death is not one a person can stand in for.

laozi-02-74b.translation: Of those who hew in place of the master carpenter, few escape cutting their own hands.
laozi-02-74b.note: The image is pushed to its end and the result written down.

laozi-02-75a.translation: The people go hungry because those above eat too much in taxes; that is why they go hungry. The people are hard to govern because those above act too much; that is why they are hard to govern. The people make light of death because those above seek their own life too thickly; that is why they make light of it.
laozi-02-75a.note: All three problems are traced to the same place: those above.

laozi-02-75b.translation: Only one who does not make a business of living is better than one who prizes life.
laozi-02-75b.note: It inverts the way of caring for one's life.

laozi-02-76a.translation: Alive, a person is soft and weak; dead, hard and stiff. Living plants and trees are soft and tender; dead, dry and brittle. So the hard and stiff belong to death, the soft and weak to life. An army that is strong does not win; a tree that is stiff gets cut.
laozi-02-76a.note: The clearest chapter for taking softness as the mark of being alive.

laozi-02-76b.translation: The strong and great take the lower place; the soft and weak take the upper.
laozi-02-76b.note: Picture a tree and the sentence is simply true.

laozi-02-77a.translation: Is heaven's way not like drawing a bow? The high is pressed down, the low is lifted; what is in excess is reduced, what is wanting is supplied. Heaven's way takes from excess to supply want. The human way is not like this: it takes from want to serve excess.
laozi-02-77a.note: It states plainly that heaven's way and the human way run opposite.

laozi-02-77b.translation: Who can take what is in excess and serve the world with it? Only one who has the way. So the sage acts and does not presume, completes the work and does not stay in it, and does not wish to be seen as worthy.
laozi-02-77b.note: The clause from chapter 2 returns near the end of the book.

laozi-02-78a.translation: Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, and nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong; nothing can take its place. That the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, everyone in the world knows, and no one can practise.
laozi-02-78a.note: Right to the end it points at the gap between knowing and doing.

laozi-02-78b.translation: So the sage says: one who takes on the filth of the state is called lord of the altars; one who takes on the state's ill fortune is called king of the world. Straight words sound inverted.
laozi-02-78b.note: The last four characters explain the style of the whole book.

laozi-02-79.translation: Reconcile a great resentment and some resentment is sure to remain; how can that be called good? So the sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press others. Those with character take charge of the tally; those without take charge of collection. Heaven's way has no favourites and is always with the good.
laozi-02-79.note: It takes the side that holds the right to collect and does not use it.

laozi-02-80a.translation: Let the state be small and the people few. Let there be tools for ten or a hundred and no use for them; let the people take death seriously and not move far away. Though there be boats and carts, no occasion to ride them; though there be armour and weapons, no occasion to draw them up.
laozi-02-80a.note: Not abolishing them: leaving no occasion to use them.

laozi-02-80b.translation: Let people go back to knotting cords and using them; let their food taste good, their clothes look fine, their dwellings be comfortable, their customs be a pleasure. Neighbouring states in sight of each other, the sound of cocks and dogs carrying across, and the people growing old and dying without going back and forth.
laozi-02-80b.note: A picture of a state in which what is one's own is taken as enough.

laozi-02-81a.translation: Words you can trust are not dressed up; dressed-up words are not to be trusted. The good do not argue; those who argue are not good. Those who know are not wide-read; the wide-read do not know. The sage does not hoard: the more he does for others the more he has, the more he gives the more there is. Heaven's way benefits and does not harm;
laozi-02-81a.note: The last chapter of the book. It opens with three matched pairs.

laozi-02-81b.translation: The sage's way: act, and do not contend.
laozi-02-81b.note: Six characters close the whole book.

sunzi-01-a.translation: War is the great affair of a state, the ground of life and death, the road to survival or ruin. It cannot go unexamined.
sunzi-01-a.note: The first sentence of a book on war does not urge war; it urges examination.

sunzi-01-b.translation: So set it out by five things, weigh it by calculation, and search out the facts: first the way, second heaven, third earth, fourth the general, fifth method.
sunzi-01-b.note: What gets measured before fighting is fixed at five items.

sunzi-01-c.translation: The way is what makes the people of one mind with those above, so they will die with them and live with them and not fear danger. Heaven is yin and yang, cold and heat, the order of seasons. Earth is high and low, far and near, steep and level, wide and narrow, ground of death and of life.
sunzi-01-c.note: The first of the five is the people's heart — not weapons, not numbers.

sunzi-01-d.translation: The general means wisdom, trustworthiness, humaneness, courage, strictness. Method means organisation, the chain of office, the management of supply. Every general has heard of these five; those who know them win, those who do not, do not.
sunzi-01-d.note: Having heard of something and knowing it are set apart — the stance of the whole book.

sunzi-01-e.translation: So weigh it by seven calculations and search out the facts: which ruler has the way? which general is abler? which side has heaven and earth? on which side are the laws carried out? which army is stronger? whose troops are better trained? whose rewards and punishments are clearer? By this I know who will win.
sunzi-01-e.note: Seven times it asks which side. Comparison is the method.
