sunzi-01-f.translation: If the general listens to my calculations, using them he will surely win, and I stay; if he does not, using them he will surely lose, and I leave. Once the calculation of advantage is accepted, make a configuration from it to help from outside. Configuration is weighing the lever according to advantage. War is a way of deception.
sunzi-01-f.note: The last clause becomes the title of everything that follows.

sunzi-01-g.translation: Able, appear unable; using, appear not to use; near, appear far; far, appear near.
sunzi-01-g.note: All four hide what you can do rather than what you cannot.

sunzi-01-h.translation: Lure them with advantage; take them when they are disordered; prepare against them when they are solid; avoid them when they are strong; provoke them and shake them; be humble and make them proud; wear them out when they are rested; split them when they are close. Attack where they are unprepared; go out where they do not expect it.
sunzi-01-h.note: Eight moves, one fitted to each state the other side can be in.

sunzi-01-i.translation: This is how the strategist wins, and it cannot be passed on in advance. The side that wins the reckoning in the temple before the fight is the side that counted more; the side that does not win it counted less. More counting wins, less counting does not — how much less no counting at all.
sunzi-01-i.note: Much of the outcome is settled by how thoroughly it was worked out beforehand.

sunzi-01-j.translation: Looking at it this way, I see who wins and who loses.
sunzi-01-j.note: Two clauses close the first chapter.

sunzi-02-a.translation: The method of using troops: a thousand fast chariots, a thousand supply carts, a hundred thousand in armour, grain carried a thousand li — the costs at home and in the field, the entertainment of envoys, materials of glue and lacquer, the upkeep of chariots and armour come to a thousand in gold a day.
sunzi-02-a.note: A book on war opens its second chapter with accounting.

sunzi-02-b.translation: Only then can an army of a hundred thousand be raised. In using it, victory is what counts; drag it out and the troops go blunt and their edge is broken; attack walls and the strength is spent; keep an army in the field long and the state's supplies fall short. Blunted troops, broken edge, spent strength, exhausted goods — and the other lords rise on your weakness.
sunzi-02-b.note: Dragging it out is feared more than losing.

sunzi-02-c.translation: Then no one, however wise, can mend what follows. So in war one hears of clumsy speed, and has never seen skilful delay. A long war that benefited the state has never existed. So one who does not fully know the harms of using troops
sunzi-02-c.note: Clumsy speed is rated above skilful delay.

sunzi-02-d.translation: cannot fully know the benefits either. One good at using troops does not conscript twice or ship grain three times; he takes equipment from home and takes grain from the enemy, and so the army has enough to eat. What impoverishes a state in war is distant transport;
sunzi-02-d.note: You cannot know the benefit, it says, without knowing the harm first.

sunzi-02-e.translation: distant transport makes the people poor. Near an army prices rise, and when prices rise the people's goods run out; when goods run out the levies press hard. Strength spent and goods exhausted, the households of the heartland stand empty. Seven in ten of the people's resources go;
sunzi-02-e.note: The cost of war is reckoned from the people's side.

sunzi-02-f.translation: broken chariots, worn horses, armour and helmets, arrows and crossbows, halberds and shields and screens, draught oxen and heavy carts take six in ten. So a wise general makes a point of feeding off the enemy: one measure of the enemy's grain is worth twenty of ours, one picul of their fodder worth twenty of ours. So what kills the enemy
sunzi-02-f.note: It offers the arithmetic: one measure of their grain equals twenty of yours.

sunzi-02-g.translation: is rage, and what takes the enemy's goods is reward. So in chariot fighting, when ten or more chariots are taken, reward the one who took the first and change their flags. Mix the chariots into your own and treat the captured soldiers well: this is called defeating the enemy and growing stronger.
sunzi-02-g.note: Treating the captured well is itself the method of growing stronger.

sunzi-02-h.translation: and does not prize a long war. So a general who knows war holds the people's fate and commands the safety of the state.
sunzi-02-h.note: The general is defined as the one holding the people's lives.

sunzi-03-a.translation: The method of using troops: to take a state whole is best, to shatter it is second; to take an army whole is best, to shatter it is second; and so for a brigade, a company, a squad.
sunzi-03-a.note: The same sentence over five units, fixing wholeness as always the better.

sunzi-03-b.translation: So a hundred victories in a hundred battles is not the finest thing; subduing the enemy's troops without fighting is. The best war attacks plans, next attacks alliances, next attacks troops, and the worst attacks walls. Attacking walls is done when there is no choice.
sunzi-03-b.note: It declares that winning every battle is not the highest thing.

sunzi-03-c.translation: Repairing shields and siege wagons and preparing the engines takes three months; raising the earthworks another three. A general who cannot master his anger sends them swarming up like ants, kills a third of his men, and still does not take the wall: this is the disaster of assault.
sunzi-03-c.note: The advice against assaulting walls comes with months and casualties attached.

sunzi-03-d.translation: So one good at using troops subdues the enemy's troops without battle, takes their walls without assault, breaks their state without a long war. He contends for the world by wholeness, so the troops are not blunted and the gain can be whole. This is the method of attacking by plan.
sunzi-03-d.note: Three times the shape: do it, but not by that means.

sunzi-03-e.translation: The method: at ten to one, surround them; at five, attack; at double, divide them; evenly matched, you can fight; fewer, you can hold; outmatched, you can avoid them. So a small force that stands firm is taken by a large one.
sunzi-03-e.note: An action is fixed for each ratio of force. Avoiding is one of the options.

sunzi-03-f.translation: The general is the support of the state. Where the support is tight, the state is strong; where there are gaps, it is weak.
sunzi-03-f.note: Two clauses bind the general to the state.

sunzi-03-g.translation: There are three ways a ruler brings trouble on his army: not knowing it cannot advance and ordering it to advance, not knowing it cannot retreat and ordering it to retreat — this is called hobbling the army;
sunzi-03-g.note: The source of the trouble is placed in the ruler.

sunzi-03-h.translation: not knowing the army's affairs and sharing in its administration, so that the soldiers are confused; not knowing the army's weighing of options and sharing in its command, so that the soldiers doubt.
sunzi-03-h.note: The result of interference is written as confusion and doubt.

sunzi-03-i.translation: With the army confused and doubting, trouble from the other lords arrives: this is called throwing your own army into disorder and handing over the victory.
sunzi-03-i.note: Disordering your own army is what manufactures the other side's win.

sunzi-03-j.translation: There are five ways to know victory: knowing when you can fight and when you cannot; knowing the use of many and few; above and below wanting the same thing; being prepared and waiting for the unprepared; a general who is able and a ruler who does not interfere. These five are the way of knowing victory.
sunzi-03-j.note: The fifth of the five is the ruler's restraint.

sunzi-03-k.translation: So it is said: know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you are never in danger; not knowing the other but knowing yourself, you win one and lose one; knowing neither, every battle is dangerous.
sunzi-03-k.note: The best-known passage in the book. All three cases are written out, so it reads as a ratio.

sunzi-04-a.translation: Those of old who fought well first made themselves unbeatable and waited for the enemy to become beatable. Being unbeatable rests with you; being beatable rests with the enemy. So one who fights well can make himself unbeatable and cannot make the enemy surely beatable.
sunzi-04-a.note: It draws a clear line between what is in your hands and what is not.

sunzi-04-b.translation: So it is said: victory can be known and cannot be made. When you cannot win, defend; when you can, attack. Defending is for insufficiency, attacking for surplus. One good at defending hides as if nine layers underground;
sunzi-04-b.note: Attack and defence are not choices but consequences of your state.

sunzi-04-c.translation: One good at attacking moves as if from nine layers of heaven, and so protects himself and wins whole. To see the victory no further than the crowd sees it is not the finest; to win the battle and have the world call it good is not the finest.
sunzi-04-c.note: A victory that gets applauded is not rated highest.

sunzi-04-d.translation: Lifting an autumn hair is not called strength, seeing sun and moon is not called sharp eyes, hearing thunder is not called keen ears. What the ancients called fighting well was winning where winning was easy. So the victories of one who fights well bring no name for wisdom and no credit for courage.
sunzi-04-d.note: Having no visible achievement is itself the evidence of having done it well.

sunzi-04-e.translation: So his victories are without error. Without error means every move he makes wins, because he beats one already beaten. So one who fights well stands on ground where he cannot lose and does not miss the moment the enemy loses.
sunzi-04-e.note: Beating one who has already lost is the core of this chapter.

sunzi-04-f.translation: So a winning army wins first and then seeks battle; a losing army fights first and then seeks to win. One good at using troops cultivates the way and keeps to method, and so can govern victory and defeat.
sunzi-04-f.note: A single difference of order separates the winning army from the losing one.

sunzi-04-g.translation: In the art of war: first measuring, second estimating, third counting, fourth weighing, fifth victory. Ground gives rise to measuring, measuring to estimating, estimating to counting, counting to weighing, weighing to victory. So a winning army is like weighing grains against pounds, a losing one like weighing pounds against grains.
sunzi-04-g.note: Victory is placed at the end of a chain of measurement.

sunzi-04-h.translation: The way a winner sends his people into battle is like releasing pent-up water down a gorge a thousand fathoms deep: that is form.
sunzi-04-h.note: The chapter closes on a single image: stored water let go.

sunzi-05-a.translation: Governing many as you govern few is a matter of division and numbers; fighting with many as with few is a matter of signals and flags; making the host of three armies able to meet the enemy without defeat is a matter of the odd and the straight;
sunzi-05-a.note: A problem of scale is solved by organisation and signalling.

sunzi-05-b.translation: Troops falling like a grindstone on an egg is a matter of emptiness and fullness. In battle you meet with the straight and win with the odd. One good at producing the odd is endless as heaven and earth, inexhaustible as rivers and sea. Ending and beginning again, like sun and moon.
sunzi-05-b.note: A surprise only works once the straightforward part is solid.

sunzi-05-c.translation: Dying and living again, like the four seasons. There are no more than five notes, and the changes of the five cannot all be heard; no more than five colours, and their changes cannot all be seen; no more than five flavours, and their changes cannot all be tasted;
sunzi-05-c.note: Few elements and endless combinations, shown three times over.

sunzi-05-d.translation: The configurations of battle are no more than the odd and the straight, and their changes cannot be exhausted. Odd and straight give birth to each other like a ring without end — who could exhaust them? Rushing water so swift it rolls boulders along: that is configuration;
sunzi-05-d.note: From only two elements, endless variation.

sunzi-05-e.translation: A hawk so swift it breaks the bones of its prey: that is timing. So one who fights well has a steep configuration and a short timing. Configuration is like a drawn crossbow, timing like releasing the trigger. In the swirl and tumble of mixed fighting, he cannot be thrown into disorder;
sunzi-05-e.note: The drawn bow and the released trigger separate configuration from timing.

sunzi-05-f.translation: Blurred and confused, his formation is round and cannot be broken. Disorder is born of order, cowardice of courage, weakness of strength. Order and disorder are a matter of numbers; courage and cowardice of configuration; strength and weakness of form. So one good at moving the enemy shows them a form, and they follow it;
sunzi-05-f.note: Three pairs of opposites, each said to be born from the other.

sunzi-05-g.translation: Give them something and they take it. Move them with advantage and wait for them with troops. So one who fights well looks to configuration for the answer and does not blame his men, and so can choose men and entrust them to the configuration. Entrusting to configuration, he sends men into battle as one rolls logs and stones.
sunzi-05-g.note: Blaming people for a bad outcome leaves whatever caused it untouched.

sunzi-05-h.translation: It is the nature of logs and stones to stay still on level ground and move on a slope, to stop when square and roll when round. So the configuration of one who makes men fight well is like rolling round stones down a mountain a thousand fathoms high: that is configuration.
sunzi-05-h.note: Instead of driving people, he builds the slope they will roll down.

sunzi-06-a.translation: Whoever occupies the battleground first and waits is at ease; whoever comes late and rushes into the fight is worn out. So one who fights well brings others to him and is not brought to them. Making the enemy come of themselves is done by showing them an advantage;
sunzi-06-a.note: The whole chapter is about who holds the initiative.

sunzi-06-b.translation: and keeping them from coming is done by showing them harm. So if the enemy is at ease, wear them out; if fed, starve them; if settled, move them. Go out where they do not hurry to, hurry to where they do not expect. To march a thousand li without exhaustion is to march where there is no one.
sunzi-06-b.note: For each state the other side is in, a move to overturn it.

sunzi-06-c.translation: To attack and surely take is to attack where they do not defend; to defend and surely hold is to defend where they will not attack. So against one good at attacking, the enemy does not know where to defend; against one good at defending, they do not know where to attack. Subtle, subtle, to the point of no form;
sunzi-06-c.note: Keeping them from knowing is the method on both sides, attack and defence.

sunzi-06-d.translation: divine, divine, to the point of no sound; and so he holds the enemy's fate. Advancing and not to be blocked, he strikes at the emptiness; withdrawing and not to be pursued, he is too quick to catch.
sunzi-06-d.note: Each of unstoppable and unpursuable is given its reason.

sunzi-06-e.translation: If I want to fight, then though the enemy has high ramparts and deep ditches they cannot avoid fighting me, because I attack what they must rescue. If I do not want to fight, then though I defend a line scratched on the ground they cannot fight me, because I put them off where they were headed.
sunzi-06-e.note: Even whether the fight happens at all is decided from this side.

sunzi-06-f.translation: So make them show a form while I have none, and I am concentrated and they are divided. I am one, they are ten, and so I attack their one with ten: I am many and they are few. Able to strike few with many, what I have to fight is simple.
sunzi-06-f.note: With equal totals, you can still be the larger force where it matters.

sunzi-06-g.translation: If the ground where I will fight cannot be known, then there is much for the enemy to prepare; and with much to prepare, there are few of them where I fight.
sunzi-06-g.note: Keeping them in the dark converts directly into a difference in numbers.

sunzi-06-h.translation: Prepare the front and the rear is thin; prepare the rear and the front is thin; prepare the left and the right is thin; prepare the right and the left is thin. Prepare everywhere and everywhere is thin. The few are those who prepare against others; the many are those who make others prepare against them.
sunzi-06-h.note: The last clause redefines what many and few mean.

sunzi-06-i.translation: Know the ground of the battle and the day of the battle, and you can march a thousand li and meet for it;
sunzi-06-i.note: The first half of a pair; the second follows.

sunzi-06-j.translation: Not knowing the ground or the day, the left cannot rescue the right, the right the left, the front the rear, the rear the front — how much less when the far are tens of li apart and the near a few li.
sunzi-06-j.note: A thousand li against a few li, to show what knowing is worth.

sunzi-06-k.translation: By my reckoning, however many troops the men of Yue have, what does it add to winning or losing? So it is said: victory can be taken in hand. However many the enemy, they can be kept from fighting.
sunzi-06-k.note: The conclusion: numbers do not settle the outcome.

sunzi-06-l.translation: Reckon them and know the calculus of gain and loss; stir them and know the pattern of their movement and rest; show them a form and know the ground of death and life; probe them and know where they have surplus and where they lack. The height of giving troops a form is to arrive at no form.
sunzi-06-l.note: Four ways of probing, ending in having no form at all.

sunzi-06-m.translation: With no form, the deepest spy cannot peer in and the wisest cannot plan against you. Following their form you set victory before the crowd, and the crowd cannot see it. Everyone knows the form by which I won; no one knows the form by which I made the winning.
sunzi-06-m.note: The result is visible; the process is not.

sunzi-06-n.translation: So his victories are never repeated; he answers forms without end. The form of troops is like water: water avoids the high and runs to the low; troops avoid the full and strike the empty. Water shapes its course by the ground; troops shape their victory by the enemy.
sunzi-06-n.note: Never using the same method twice is this chapter's conclusion.

sunzi-06-o.translation: So troops have no fixed configuration and no constant form. One who can change with the enemy and take the victory is called divine. Among the five phases none always wins; among the four seasons none holds its place; days are short and long, and the moon dies and lives.
sunzi-06-o.note: The chapter closes by saying there is no fixed answer.

sunzi-07-a.translation: Of all that a general does — receiving the command, assembling the army, gathering the host, facing the enemy and encamping — nothing is harder than contending for position. What makes it hard is making the roundabout the direct and turning trouble into advantage.
sunzi-07-a.note: It opens on the paradox that going around can be the shorter road.

sunzi-07-b.translation: So he goes by a roundabout road and lures them with advantage, sets out after them and arrives before them: this is knowing the calculus of the roundabout and the direct. Contending for position is advantage, and contending for position is danger. Move the whole army to contend and you do not arrive; leave the army behind to contend and the baggage is lost.
sunzi-07-b.note: It writes advantage on one line and danger on the next.

sunzi-07-c.translation: So rolling up the armour and hurrying, not halting day or night, doubling the marches to contend for advantage a hundred li off, the generals of all three armies are captured: the strong get there first and the worn out lag, and by that rule one in ten arrives;
sunzi-07-c.note: For each distance, the arrival rate is given as a number.

sunzi-07-d.translation: contending fifty li off, the general of the vanguard falls and half arrive; thirty li off, two thirds arrive. So an army without baggage is lost, without provisions is lost, without stores is lost.
sunzi-07-d.note: A tenth at a hundred li, half at fifty, two thirds at thirty.

sunzi-07-e.translation: Not knowing the other lords' plans, you cannot make alliances in advance; not knowing the shape of mountains and woods, defiles and marshes, you cannot march an army; not using local guides, you cannot take the advantage of the ground.
sunzi-07-e.note: For each of three kinds of ignorance, a thing you cannot do.

sunzi-07-f.translation: Troops are established by deception, moved by advantage, varied by dividing and joining. So swift as wind, slow as forest, raiding like fire, unmoving as a mountain, hard to read as shadow, moving like thunder.
sunzi-07-f.note: Known as wind-forest-fire-mountain, though the list actually has six items.

sunzi-07-g.translation: Taking a district, share it among the host; widening the ground, share the gain; hang the scales before moving. Whoever first knows the calculus of the roundabout and the direct wins: this is the method of contending for position.
sunzi-07-g.note: Sharing out is written down as a tactical item.

sunzi-07-h.translation: The Book of Army Administration says: speech is not heard across the ranks, so there are gongs and drums; sight does not carry, so there are flags and banners. Gongs, drums, flags and banners are what make the ears and eyes of the host one.
sunzi-07-h.note: The purpose of the signalling gear is to make them one.

sunzi-07-i.translation: Once the host is made one, the brave cannot advance alone and the timid cannot retreat alone: this is the method of using many. So in night fighting use many gongs and drums, in day fighting many flags, because they change what people's ears and eyes take in.
sunzi-07-i.note: Holding back the brave is counted as part of command too.

sunzi-07-j.translation: An army can be robbed of its spirit, a general of his resolve. Morning spirit is keen, midday spirit slack, evening spirit bent on going home. So one good at using troops avoids the keen spirit and strikes the slack and homeward: this is governing spirit.
sunzi-07-j.note: The rise and fall within a single day is used to pick the moment.

sunzi-07-k.translation: Meet disorder with order, clamour with stillness: this is governing the mind. Meet the far with the near, the worn with the rested, the hungry with the fed: this is governing strength. Do not meet well-ordered banners or strike a formation in full array: this is governing change.
sunzi-07-k.note: Four groupings: governing spirit, mind, strength and change.

sunzi-07-l.translation: Do not attack uphill, do not meet an enemy with a hill at their back, do not pursue a feigned flight, do not attack keen troops, do not swallow bait troops, do not block an army going home, always leave a gap when you surround, do not press a cornered enemy.
sunzi-07-l.note: All eight are prohibitions. The last two are the best known.

sunzi-08-a.translation: When the general has his command and the army is assembled: on broken ground do not camp; on crossroads ground make alliances; on cut-off ground do not linger; on enclosed ground, plan; on death ground, fight.
sunzi-08-a.note: For each of five terrains, one thing to do.

sunzi-08-b.translation: There are roads not to take, armies not to strike, walled towns not to assault, ground not to contend for, and commands of the ruler not to accept. A general who sees through to the advantages of the nine changes knows how to use troops;
sunzi-08-b.note: Not accepting the ruler's order is listed as the fifth item.

sunzi-08-c.translation: A general who does not see through them, though he knows the terrain, cannot take the ground's advantage; one who governs troops without the art of the nine changes, though he knows the ground's advantage, cannot get the use of his men.
sunzi-08-c.note: Another step is placed between knowing and using.

sunzi-08-d.translation: So the wise always mix advantage and harm in their deliberations: mixing harm into advantage, the undertaking can be relied on; mixing advantage into harm, the trouble can be undone. So bend the other lords with harm, keep them busy with tasks, and make them hurry to you with advantage.
sunzi-08-d.note: Not looking only at the advantage becomes the definition of wisdom.

sunzi-08-e.translation: The method of using troops: do not count on their not coming — count on being ready for them; do not count on their not attacking — count on there being nothing in you that can be attacked.
sunzi-08-e.note: Preparation rests on what you have done, not on what you hope they will not do.

sunzi-08-f.translation: A general has five dangers: bent on death, he can be killed; bent on living, he can be captured; quick to rage, he can be provoked; too scrupulous, he can be shamed; loving the people, he can be harassed. These five are a general's faults and a disaster in using troops.
sunzi-08-f.note: Two of the five look like virtues, and are listed among the dangers anyway.

sunzi-08-g.translation: Armies are overturned and generals killed by these five dangers without fail. They cannot go unexamined.
sunzi-08-g.note: The line from the first chapter, that it cannot go unexamined, returns here.

sunzi-09-a.translation: In placing an army and watching the enemy: crossing mountains, keep to the valleys; look for living ground and stay high; do not climb to fight an enemy above you. This is placing an army in mountains. Crossing water, get well away from it; when the enemy crosses toward you, do not meet them in the water — let half of them cross and then strike; that is to your advantage.
sunzi-09-a.note: How to place yourself on each terrain. The line about striking at the halfway crossing is well known.

sunzi-09-b.translation: If you mean to fight, do not meet them pressed against the water; look for living ground and stay high; do not face upstream. This is placing an army by water.
sunzi-09-b.note: The same pattern continues through four terrains.

sunzi-09-c.translation: Crossing marshes, get away quickly and do not linger; if you meet an army in the middle of a marsh, keep to water and grass with woods at your back. This is placing an army in marshes. On level ground, take the easy footing with high ground at your right rear, dead ground in front and living ground behind. This is placing an army on the plain.
sunzi-09-c.note: Four terrains closed off with the same sentence pattern.

sunzi-09-d.translation: These four advantages of placement are how the Yellow Emperor beat the four emperors. Armies prefer high ground to low, prize sun over shade, nurture life and settle on solid ground; then the army is free of the hundred ailments, and this is called sure victory.
sunzi-09-d.note: Freedom from sickness is counted among the conditions for winning.

sunzi-09-e.translation: On hills and embankments, keep to the sunny side with them at your right rear: this is the advantage of troops and the help of the ground. When rain has fallen upstream and foam comes down, anyone meaning to ford should wait for it to settle.
sunzi-09-e.note: Waiting is written down as one of the tactical items.

sunzi-09-f.translation: Where there are sheer ravines, heaven's well, heaven's prison, heaven's net, heaven's pit, heaven's crevice, get away quickly and do not go near. Keep them at a distance and let the enemy come near them; face them yourself and let the enemy have them at their back.
sunzi-09-f.note: Six named kinds of ground to avoid.

sunzi-09-g.translation: Where there are defiles, pools, reed beds, woods or thick cover beside your army, search them again and again: this is where ambushes and spies lie. The enemy close by and quiet are trusting to their ground; challenging from far off, they want you to come forward;
sunzi-09-g.note: From here a long list begins: reading the enemy's signs.

sunzi-09-h.translation: Settled on easy ground, there is an advantage in it; trees stirring, they are coming; many screens set in the grass, they want you suspicious; birds rising, an ambush; beasts startled, a sweep coming; dust rising high and sharp, chariots; low and wide, infantry;
sunzi-09-h.note: The shape of the dust tells you which arm is coming.

sunzi-09-i.translation: dust scattered in streaks, they are gathering firewood; a little coming and going, they are making camp. Humble words with increased preparation mean an advance; strong words and a show of pressing forward mean a retreat; light chariots out first and taking the flanks means they are forming up;
sunzi-09-i.note: A mismatch between what is said and what is done is read as the signal.

sunzi-09-j.translation: asking for peace without terms means a scheme; running about and drawing up troops means a time has been set; half advancing and half withdrawing means a lure. Leaning on their spears means hunger; drawing water and drinking first means thirst; seeing an advantage and not taking it means exhaustion;
sunzi-09-j.note: From the soldiers' gestures, the state of their supply.

sunzi-09-k.translation: birds gathering means the camp is empty; calling out at night means fear; disturbance in the camp means the general carries no weight; flags shifting means disorder; officers angry means weariness; feeding grain to the horses and eating meat, with no cooking pots hung and no return to quarters, means a cornered enemy;
sunzi-09-k.note: Birds settling tells you the camp has been abandoned.

sunzi-09-l.translation: muttering together and speaking slowly means he has lost the host; frequent rewards mean he is at his wit's end; frequent punishments mean he is in difficulty; being violent first and then fearing his own men is the height of imprecision; coming to make apologies means they want a rest.
sunzi-09-l.note: Frequent rewards and frequent punishments are both read as bad signs.

sunzi-09-m.translation: When troops face each other in anger and neither closes nor withdraws for a long time, look into it carefully. Troops are not prized for being more numerous; not advancing recklessly, concentrating strength, sizing up the enemy and winning people is enough.
sunzi-09-m.note: Not numbers but three activities are said to be enough.

sunzi-09-n.translation: One who is thoughtless and makes light of the enemy is sure to be captured. Punish soldiers before they are attached to you and they will not submit; not submitting, they are hard to use. Let punishment lapse once they are attached and they cannot be used.
sunzi-09-n.note: The timing of punishment is matched to the stage of the relationship.

sunzi-09-o.translation: So command them with culture and align them with discipline: this is called sure success. Teach the people while orders are habitually carried out and they submit; teach them while orders are habitually ignored and they do not. Orders habitually carried out means you and the host have come to terms.
sunzi-09-o.note: The word habitually appears three times. It is not something produced in a crisis.

sunzi-10-a.translation: Terrain may be open, entangling, deadlocked, narrow, steep, or distant. Where I can go and they can come is called open.
sunzi-10-a.note: The six terrains are named up front.

sunzi-10-b.translation: On open ground, take the high sunny side first and keep the supply road clear; then fighting is to your advantage. Where you can go but return is hard is called entangling. There, if the enemy is unprepared you go out and beat them; if they are prepared you go out and do not win, and return is hard — not to your advantage.
sunzi-10-b.note: Whether you can get back is reckoned separately.

sunzi-10-c.translation: Where neither side gains by going out is called deadlocked. There, though the enemy dangles an advantage, do not go out; draw off instead, and strike when they are half out — that is to your advantage. On narrow ground, occupy it first and fill it to wait for them.
sunzi-10-c.note: A case where not going out is itself the move.

sunzi-10-d.translation: If the enemy occupies it first and fills it, do not follow; if they have not filled it, follow. On steep ground, occupy it first and wait on the high sunny side; if they occupy it first, draw off and do not follow.
sunzi-10-d.note: The answer turns on which side got there first.

sunzi-10-e.translation: On distant ground the forces are even, it is hard to provoke a fight, and fighting is not to your advantage. These six are the way of the ground and the general's highest charge; they cannot go unexamined.
sunzi-10-e.note: The phrase cannot go unexamined turns up again.

sunzi-10-f.translation: Armies may bolt, slacken, sink, collapse, fall into disorder, or be routed. These six are not heaven's disasters but the general's faults. With forces even, to strike ten with one is called bolting;
sunzi-10-f.note: All six failures are assigned to the general.

sunzi-10-g.translation: strong soldiers and weak officers is called slackening; strong officers and weak soldiers is called sinking; senior officers angry and insubordinate, meeting the enemy and fighting on their own out of resentment while the general does not know their capacity, is called collapse;
sunzi-10-g.note: The kinds of failure are sorted by combinations of strong and weak.

sunzi-10-h.translation: a general weak and lax, teaching unclear, officers and men inconsistent, the formation sprawling, is called disorder; a general unable to size up the enemy, pitting few against many and weak against strong, with no picked vanguard, is called rout.
sunzi-10-h.note: Through the sixth, every one is something the general failed to do.

sunzi-10-i.translation: These six are the road to defeat and the general's highest charge; they cannot go unexamined. Terrain is an aid to troops. Sizing up the enemy and making the victory, reckoning the steep and the narrow, the far and the near, is the way of a superior general.
sunzi-10-i.note: Terrain is placed as an aid, not the main actor.

sunzi-10-j.translation: One who knows this and fights surely wins; one who does not surely loses. So if the logic of the battle is sure victory, you may fight though the ruler says not to; if it is not, you may refrain though he says you must.
sunzi-10-j.note: Both directions of disobeying the ruler are written out.

sunzi-10-k.translation: So advancing he does not seek fame, withdrawing he does not avoid blame; he looks only to protecting the people, and if the benefit matches the ruler's, he is the treasure of the state. Look on your soldiers as infants and they will go with you into the deepest gorge; look on them as beloved sons and they will die with you.
sunzi-10-k.note: How the soldiers are treated becomes the fighting strength itself.

sunzi-10-l.translation: Generous and unable to employ them, loving and unable to command them, disorderly and unable to govern them — they are like spoiled children and cannot be used. To know your own troops can strike and not know the enemy cannot be struck is half a victory;
sunzi-10-l.note: A condition is attached immediately to the affection of the line before.

sunzi-10-m.translation: to know the enemy can be struck and not know your own troops cannot is half a victory; to know both and not know the terrain does not allow a fight is half a victory.
sunzi-10-m.note: Half repeated three times. Only knowing all three makes it whole.

sunzi-10-n.translation: So one who knows war moves without confusion and acts without running out. So it is said: know the other and know yourself, and the victory is not in danger; know heaven and know earth, and the victory can be whole.
sunzi-10-n.note: The line from Book 3, closed off with one more about heaven and earth.
